channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Hermès Foundation Missulsang Launches Digital Archive Spanning 25 Years
item.description: K-ARTNOW: “On September 1, the Hermès Foundation unveiled a digital archive commemorating the 20th edition of the Hermès Foundation Missulsang, titled Memories for the Future: 25 Years of Hermès Foundation Missulsang. Since 2000, the Missulsang has sought out and supported new practices and experiments in Korean contemporary art.”

item.title: The Met is now on Unsplash
item.description: Unsplash: “The Met launch includes 1000 images, and highlights a range of its museums and archives, each bringing a completely different lens on art history, costume and textile history and cultures. These 10 collections span some of hundreds of the institution’s most iconic departments and artists.”

item.title: Nitter and XCancel are dead (again) after X’s latest legal actions
item.description: TechCrunch: “After X threatened legal action last month, Nitter and XCancel, privacy-friendly services for viewing X posts, appear to be officially dead — for real this time.”

item.title: ‘Mama, I Miss You’: Relatives Go Online to Grieve Tibet’s Flood Victims.
item.description: New York Times: “Nearly two weeks have passed since a fierce deluge of ice, boulders and mud tore through a border complex in Tibet, but China has not released an official list of those missing. In the information void, people have found their own ways to seek help and vent their grief.”

item.title: I fixed a tractor using John Deere’s self-repair service. Farmers aren’t sold on it.
item.description: Ars Technica: “Over the last decade, John Deere has become a big target of the ever-growing right-to-repair movement. The company’s high-tech software systems also come equipped with digital locks, which require official, dealer-sanctioned approval to access. If you want to fiddle with a part, or replace it with an aftermarket alternative, those software restrictions can block those attempts.”

item.title: Planned Archives Closures Raise Alarm Over Tribal Records
item.description: The Circle News: “Tribal advocates argue that relocating these materials without consultation disregards the federal government’s trust responsibility and its nation-to-nation relationship with tribes. Some tribal governments and coalitions have requested greater transparency, while advocates are calling for congressional intervention and possible legal action.”

item.title: Culture ministry official rejects Thai claim Preah Vihear was used as military base
item.description: Khmer Times: “A Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts official has rejected Thailand’s allegation that Preah Vihear Temple was used as a Cambodian military base, saying the UNESCO-listed site has been dedicated to cultural, religious, conservation, research and educational purposes and that any claims of military use should be independently verified.”

item.title: Acme Design surprises world’s youngest museum curator with T. rex skull replica
item.description: Kewanee Voice: “Museum founder and curator, Anderson Taylor, first met members of the Acme Design team at the Association of Midwest Museums conference last year. They remembered Anderson and his remarkable story and recently visited the museum to surprise him with the skull.”

item.title: Removing algorithmic feed slop from my life
item.description: Andy Bell: “I decided to cut loose. I deleted Instagram, TikTok and Bluesky from my phone because I don’t use anything else. The feeling I had, for the first couple of days after that was the exact same feeling I had in attempts to quit nicotine, which was rather concerning. I persisted though, leaning more and more into my beloved RSS feeds whenever I had a pang to pick up my phone and scroll.”

item.title: Aw shucks: Dolly Parton corn mazes crop up in fields nationwide
item.description: Associated Press: “Dolly Parton ’s megawatt smile and big wavy locks are gracing fields across the U.S. and Canada this fall. Twenty farms have carved out large corn mazes to honor the late country music icon, actor and philanthropist and raise money for her Imagination Library, which provides free books to children.”

item.title: This group is building benches at bus stops that don’t have one. Will the city let them?
item.description: Chicago Sun-Times: “A pair of homemade wooden benches painted bright yellow and blue appeared last week at CTA bus stops in Ukrainian Village. The benches were built and installed by a neighborhood group tired of seeing bus stops without them. Several people posting online praised the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance for building the benches. The group wants to build more, but is waiting to see what the city does. Technically, the benches are illegal.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Mercyhurst marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 with new Homeland Security Collection
item.description: Mercyhurst University: “On the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, Mercyhurst University is launching a new digital archival collection documenting an important chapter in the nation’s response to 9/11: the creation of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties (CRCL).”

item.title: GROOVE PROTOCOL PRESENTS CULTURE: Digital Archive of Croatian Electronic Music Scene
item.description: INSITE: “In a selfless attempt to keep all the information regarding the progress, impact and evolution of Croatian electronic music scene, three individuals have come together and created a new platform called Culture, imagined as its official archive.”

item.title: An oral history project captures stories in and around K-Town. Now anyone can dive in
item.description: LAist: “Lauren Kim works alongside her father, Hanjik, at his traditional medicine clinic on the border of Koreatown and MacArthur Park. But it took an oral history interview for her to hear parts of his story for the first time…. Now that interview, along with hundreds of others about life in and around Koreatown, is being gathered into the new K-Town Archive in a partnership with UCLA that also collects photographs and ephemera.”

item.title: Windows 11 can now reinstall itself from the cloud, no USB stick required
item.description: TechSpot: “Windows 11 Insider Beta Preview Build 26220.9343 introduces a new reinitialization option that downloads a factory version of the OS from the cloud. The new feature lets users and IT administrators reset a device without needing a USB stick or a custom image.”

item.title: LG Denies Its TVs Are Spying on You (Unless You Opted In)
item.description: Gizmodo: “LG is pushing back against claims that its TVs eavesdrop on owners constantly after a joint report by Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs discovered unsettling details about how much data it phones home—including when the devices are offline or in standby mode.”

item.title: I went looking for obscure open-source apps and found 6 that are way too good to be this unknown
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I like open-source software, but recommendation lists tend to circle the same dozen apps until you could name them from memory. So I went further down the rabbit hole, through smaller GitHub projects, niche recommendation threads, and apps that barely seem to exist outside their communities. The search turned up a much less familiar collection.”

item.title: The Vatican Library and Apostolic Archive will have a new building inside Vatican City
item.description: Infovaticana: “Pope Leo XIV has ordered the construction of a new building within Vatican City primarily intended to expand the spaces of the Vatican Apostolic Library and the Vatican Apostolic Archive, after the growth of their collections has rendered the currently available facilities insufficient.”

item.title: Post Peek
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: a Chrome and Firefox extension called “Read one X post and leave. A Chrome and Firefox (Manifest V3) extension that opens x.com and twitter.com post links in a popup instead of sending you to the full site.”

item.title: Indian police to query Google over 500,000 fake Gmail IDs linked to bomb hoax
item.description: Reuters: “Indian police will question Google over a lack ​of safeguards after smashing a criminal network that set up and managed more than ‌500,000 fake Gmail accounts to send hoax bomb threats to government offices, a police official told Reuters on Tuesday.”

item.title: The High Crime of “LMAO”: How Cops Are Treating Mass Surveillance As a Joke
item.description: EFF: “When law enforcement and tech salespeople pitch ALPRs to city councils, they stick to a familiar script. They trumpet the technology, which is often provided by private companies like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, or Axon, as an essential tool for solving high-stakes crimes, such as car jacking, kidnapping, or murder. But when you strip away the carefully curated talking points, the data continues to reveal a different (and frankly, ridiculous) story.”

item.title: How cellphone data can help airports improve the travel experience
item.description: Texas A&M: “Researchers use mobile network signals to build a forecasting model that predicts crowds, cuts congestion and emissions and drives staffing and transit decisions.”

item.title: Spotlight Delaware launches Campaign Finance Explorer
item.description: Spotlight Delaware: “Spotlight Delaware has launched the Delaware Campaign Finance Explorer, a free, easy-to-use tool for the public to see who is funding candidates running for state and county offices this year.”

item.title: “It’s Like An Addiction”: The Man Archiving Pirate Radio Station Kool FM
item.description: New-to-me, from Londonist: “First broadcasting on 28 November 1991, Kool FM quickly rose to the top of London’s pirate radio scene. As the jungle genre grew in 1992/1993 — then exploded in 1994 — Kool was at the forefront. It continues to this day under the Rinse umbrella. Here, curator of the Original Kool Archives, Trevor 7oaks, explains his life-long infatuation with the station, and his self-appointed mission to archive as much of it as possible.”

item.title: YouTube’s new public viewcounts over-report actual engagement by 40%
item.description: Tubefilter: “YouTube‘s new public viewcounts over-report engagement by 40%, according to new data from Agentio. As you probably know, YouTube last month introduced a significant change to how it counts views on long-form content. Instead of requiring people to watch for a certain length of time before considering them ‘a viewer’ (the amount has never been publicly disclosed, but word on the street is it’s about 30 seconds), YouTube decided it will count a view from the instant a video’s first frame loads.”

item.title: Kagi Translate is back
item.description: Kagi Blog: “Today, Kagi Translate is moving to a freemium model and launching a new standalone Individual subscription for $8/month. Anyone with a Kagi account can continue using Translate for free with a limited monthly allowance. For people who use it more regularly, the new Individual plan includes all Kagi Translate features. Translate will also continue to be included with the Kagi Ultimate plan.”

item.title: Internet Archive Receives IMLS Grant to Expand Access to Local and State Government Information
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “Internet Archive has received funding from the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) to support the development of ATLAS (Access To Local And State government information), a digital preservation program for state and local government agencies.”

item.title: Korea uses fantasy video game to drive real-world tourism
item.description: Korea Times: “The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) on Monday announced a partnership with NEXON Games, one of the nation’s premier game developers. Under the partnership, the state agency will open its vast, high-definition digital archive — comprising roughly 71,000 expert-vetted photos and video assets — to assist developers in sculpting realistic virtual landscapes of Korea.”

item.title: Advertisers report Google Ads credits being revoked after spending
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Some Google Ads promotional credits are reportedly being invalidated after advertisers have already spent the amount required to qualify, potentially leaving businesses with higher advertising costs than they expected…. PPC consultant David Melamed said he has encountered the issue twice in a short period.”

item.title: Doctor Doom Shows Up to Support Seattle’s Surveillance Network
item.description: Gizmodo: “Ahead of the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie, its titular supervillain apparently made a stop at Seattle City Council this week to endorse the city’s growing surveillance network.”

item.title: Psychologists find smartphone screenshots can cause a profound degree of “digital amnesia”
item.description: PsyPost: “New research suggests that taking a screenshot of an image on your smartphone makes you less likely to remember it later, without providing any compensatory boost to your mental bandwidth. A series of experiments indicates that the simple act of capturing an image on a screen triggers a lasting inattention to that experience, leaving people with worse memory for what they just saw. These findings were published in Memory & Cognition.”

item.title: Record number of museums awarded Designated status
item.description: Museums Journal: “A record nine museums, libraries and archives have been awarded Designated status for their collections – which span film memorabilia, the archive of a medieval monastery and documents detailing the design, construction and operation of the world’s first underwater tunnel. The Designation scheme was first launched in 1997 to recognise and celebrate collections of national and international importance, and was relaunched by Arts Council England (ACE) in 2024 with a new focus on the place-based significance of collections.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Center for Energy Law and Policy’s Michael Helbing and Hannah Wiseman release Solar Ordinance Database
item.description: Penn State: “The Penn State Center for Energy Law and Policy has published a user-friendly Pennsylvania solar ordinance database. The database includes filters for a variety of provisions in local government ordinances addressing grid-scale solar development…. The database contains 4,900 ordinance provisions from 300 local governments across 57 counties.”

item.title: One Dude Mapped Route 66 in Its Entirety, and You Can Scroll Through All 2,199 Miles
item.description: The Drive: “Jake Boyles is the developer of the Pit Stop: Road Trip Exit Guide app, which shows restaurants and other points of interest located near highway exits. He spent this past summer mapping Route 66 to create a version of the app specifically for the historic highway. It lets you scroll through all 2,199 miles, showing elevation changes and places to stop along the way.”

item.title: New Mexico Department of Justice presents Mark Zuckerberg deposition in state’s Facebook case
item.description: Source New Mexico: “New Mexico Department of Justice attorneys led the second day of the state’s trial against Facebook by showing the jury a video deposition of founder Mark Zuckerberg regarding allegations that his company’s leaders publicly misrepresented how they stored and shared users’ data.”

item.title: Panic builds over bankrupt Spirit’s looming data sale to Google
item.description: Ars Technica: “Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings. Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally.”

item.title: Introducing mapsnap: Automated Georeferencing for Historic Sanborn Insurance Maps
item.description: Danvk: “It is, for the most part, possible to automaticallly georeference Sanborn maps. Some maps are harder than others and it doesn’t get everything right, but it generally does a good job. My program to automatically georeference Sanborn maps is called mapsnap, and I’m excited to explain how it works!”

item.title: Ten Resources Debunking September 11 Conspiracy Theories
item.description: Council on Foreign Relations: “Left unrebutted, conspiracy theories can extend their reach, especially through social media as new generations of Americans come of age. So, if you doubt the official story of the September 11 attacks, or know someone who does, check out one or more of the ten resources below. Three are books and reports, two are articles, four are video documentaries, and one is a radio show.”

item.title: IMDb’s “digital creator” label lets artists “represent the full scope of their work in one place”
item.description: Tubefilter: “The Internet Movie Database is as old as the World Wide Web itself, and as it enters its 36th year of activity, it is getting an important update. For the first time, the website known as IMDb is adding labels that identify various types of digital creators.”

item.title: China, US pledge to work with Cambodia on cultural heritage preservation
item.description: Khmer Times: “The embassies of China and the United States in Cambodia have announced continued cooperation with Cambodian authorities to promote cultural heritage preservation, including antiquity restoration, joint archaeological research and human resource development.”

item.title: A Pint Near Me – what you do after 15 seconds of fame
item.description: KnowWhere: “After I had got over my 15 seconds of relative fame, I wondered whether I could do something better mapping pubs in the UK. I asked my new friend Claude Code what we could do with the FHRS data and the pubs data on OSM, a good bit of whirring and numerous back and forths and data testing/verification and we had a data pipeline.”

item.title: Buffalo Bill Center of the West Authenticates Trove of Historic Early 1800s Medals
item.description: Buffalo Bill Center of the West: “Following a thorough course of testing and analysis carried out earlier this year, the Buffalo Bill Center of the West has definitively authenticated a trove of rare and historically significant medals tied to key periods and events in the history of the American West spanning more than 100 years.”

item.title: The 92-Year-Old Mathematician and the Teenage Apprentice
item.description: New York Times: “Joan Birman thought her major discoveries were behind her. Then came an email from a young neighbor — a girl who knew little but wanted to learn.” This is a great read. Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Announcing Our New JSTOR Digital Collections Portal!
item.description: Stony Brook University: “Stony Brook University Libraries is thrilled to announce a major milestone in our ongoing mission to preserve, digitize, and share our cultural heritage collections with the world: our brand-new JSTOR Digital Collections portal is live! Through this portal, three of our collections are now freely accessible on JSTOR.org, connecting global researchers, students, and community members to these important primary sources.”

item.title: Despite Pledges From Musk, Child Sexual Abuse Material Persists on X
item.description: New York Times: “Elon Musk has long vowed to remove child sexual abuse material on his social media platform, X. But some of the content continues to appear. A review by the Canadian Center for Child Protection found that the site’s own artificial intelligence chatbot, Grok, responded to requests from users by creating dozens of sexualized and sometimes sexually explicit photos of children, including victims previously known to law enforcement, at the beginning of the year. The images included children in sexualized poses with partially exposed genitals, in states of undress and with fluid on their faces.”

item.title: Roblox expands tools to help creators build, distribute games
item.description: Reuters: “Roblox plans to let creators distribute their games as standalone apps across mobile, PC and consoles, ​the company said at its developers conference ‌on Friday, as it seeks to make games easier to access beyond the Roblox app.”

item.title: YouTube wants creators to pitch brands with guesstimated TV co-viewership stats
item.description: Tubefilter: “YouTube has come up with another way to pump viewcounts. Just a few weeks after announcing it would start counting a ‘view’ from the very first frame of a video, YouTube has added a new metric called Views (Co-Viewed) that ‘estimates’ when multiple people are watching YouTube content together on one TV screen.”

item.title: Yale Tracking Of Ukrainian Children Taken By Russia At Risk As US Reshapes $25M Program
item.description: Radio Free Europe: “Researchers at Yale University’s Humanitarian Research Lab working to track Ukrainian children forcibly transferred to Russia and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine could see their positions eliminated by December unless new funding is secured, the lab’s executive director told RFE/RL. The warning comes as the US State Department moves to restructure a $25 million program that the Yale lab was among the organizations competing for.”

item.title: Broken gadget? The EU’s repair directive makes manufacturers fix it
item.description: Euronews: “Every year, Europeans throw out millions of tonnes of electronic waste, much of it repairable. The EU’s Right to Repair Directive, passed this summer, applies across all 27 member states and pushes manufacturers to make repairs easier than replacement.”

item.title: How to detect information voids using longitudinal data from social media and web searches
item.description: Scientific Reports: “The model of the attention economy, where content producers compete for the attention of users, relies on two key forces: information supply and demand. This study leverages the feedback loop between these forces to develop a method for detecting and quantifying information voids, i.e., periods in which little or no reliable information is available on a given topic.”

item.title: Brooklyn Public Library launches first ever craft library
item.description: Gothamist: “The Brooklyn Public Library will launch its first-ever craft library on Wednesday, allowing library cardholders to borrow art supplies for a variety of activities, including screen printing, bookbinding, metal stamping and hand embroidery. The program is the passion project of Jess Harwick, a craft-loving BPL librarian of eight years.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: The Eleventh of September
item.description: Found in my RSS Feeds: the This site was first launched in 2006, went offline eventually, and was brought back online recently. “The Eleventh of September is a memorial by Tape Art. The artists created 490 drawings of life-sized figures using the temporary medium of tape. Each figure is dedicated to one person killed on September 11, 2001 at the World Trade Center, and remembers others. Search for a name, or choose a heart on the map to follow the figures through the city.”

item.title: Library Makes Nearly 500 First-Hand 9/11 Responder Accounts Available Online
item.description: Library of Congress: “The Library of Congress has launched an online collection of nearly 500 first-hand accounts from 9/11 responders to mark the 25th anniversary of the World Trade Center attack. Housed in the American Folklife Center, the collection includes 484 full-length video interviews conducted between April 2010 and September 2024, along with their corresponding transcripts, which document what responders witnessed, why they responded, what they endured, and how the experience affected their health, families and lives in the years that followed.”

item.title: Project digitally recreates a buried World War I battlefield
item.description: Virginia Tech: “The Applied Research in Immersive Experiences and Simulations (ARIES) team in University Libraries at Virginia Tech created an immersive digital experience that allows researchers and the public to explore Hill 80, a German stronghold and trench fortress near Wijtschate, Belgium, captured during the 1917 Battle of Messines.”

item.title: GTA Vice City and GTA III return to web browsers after a DMCA takedown — Open-source reverse engineering brings the classics to the web with over 100 FPS performance
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City has cemented itself as one of the most legendary games of all time. It originally came out in 2002 on the PS2 before making its way to the Xbox and PC a year later. Fast forward to 2026, and now the game is entirely playable in a browser window. It was actually already playable last year on DOS Zone but was quickly shut down following a DMCA strike from Take-Two. However, a different website called ‘Quenq’ has taken up the mantle now, and it also hosts GTA III there.”

item.title: Crashing a Plane for Clicks: Influencers Push Shock Content to Get Views
item.description: New York Times: “Across the world, aspiring influencers trespass on skyscraper roofs. They block highway traffic. They provoke strangers in grocery stores, airports and malls. They dangle from helicopters, cranes, trains and cliffs for clips lasting only seconds. Some are arrested. Others are hospitalized. And, in tragic cases, some have died. Psychologists who study this field are not surprised.”

item.title: Google Maps Is Now Terrible: Explained
item.description: The Drive: “Have you noticed that Google Maps (or your navigation app of choice) doesn’t work as well as it used to? Maybe the quickest possible route still isn’t that quick, or those quiet backstreets that used to serve as a clever shortcut are now choked with traffic as well. It’s not your imagination. GPS-based routing apps have gotten worse, and while there is a solution, it might be more trouble than it’s worth.”

item.title: Good Stuff Strand Cam ends after 25 years, ‘swatting’ to blame
item.description: Easy Reader: “For over 25 years Good Stuff restaurant in Hermosa Beach has livestreamed a block of The Strand capturing the daily musings of passing tourists, bikers and 13th street volleyball players to online audiences worldwide. Last week, the Good Stuff Strand Cam was taken down as a safety precaution, according to Cris Bennet, the restaurant’s owner.”

item.title: Baltimore pizza shop turns to social media after its card reader was stolen. It worked.
item.description: Baltimore Banner: “… the staff looked everywhere after closing. That’s when [Hasan] Ilhan checked the security footage and saw that a group of customers, who had paid for their food, had stolen the device. The group looked young, Ilhan said. Instead of calling the police, the owners decided to try to reach them through social media. Ilhan posted a video on Sunday explaining what happened and asking the Baltimore community for help finding the card reader.”

item.title: 554 heritage sites listed, digital archive planned
item.description: The New Nation (Bangladesh): “The government has published a list of 554 gazetted immovable archaeological sites and is planning to establish a National Digital Cultural Repository to preserve and provide global access to the country’s cultural heritage. Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury disclosed the plans in Parliament on Monday during the question-and-answer session.”

item.title: New report offers lessons for preserving cultural heritage in crisis zones
item.description: King’s College London: “The report, Digital heritage preservation for vulnerable collections: Reflections on the Sudan Memory project history and inventory, was authored by Dr Laura Gibson, Senior Lecturer in Digital Content Management Education at King’s, alongside Sara El-Nager, Independent Researcher and Editor, and Dr Hannah Ishmael, Lecturer in Digital Culture & Race. It draws on 14 interviews conducted by Sara El-Nager with contributors to the Sudan Memory project, the first mass digitisation project ever undertaken in Sudan.”

item.title: America’s air monitors are disappearing, along with the power to expose polluters
item.description: Louisiana Illuminator: “Over recent decades, federal funding for public air monitoring has declined, the number of monitors has fallen, and much of the remaining equipment is aging or located far from major polluters. Now, the stakes are rising: Wildfire smoke is reaching more communities, data centers are adding pollution, and climate-driven heat waves are worsening ozone levels. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has delayed and rolled back requirements meant to hold companies accountable for their emissions.”

item.title: Bear-proof trash cans in Downtown Idaho Springs are alive with pictures of local history
item.description: Clear Creek Courant: “The trash cans in downtown Idaho Springs are barely recognizable, as such, following a city project to incorporate our history on an unlikely canvas…. The historical pictures depict the people, places, and landmarks from a century ago that are the basis of our heritage and how this historic gold mining town was born.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: This AI-Powered Archive Maps 115 Years of Swedish Political Advertising
item.description: Little Black Book: “​Propagandaindex is a new digital archive that brings together Swedish election posters from 1911 to the upcoming 2026 parliamentary election. It offers a new way to explore political communication, using AI-assisted analysis to reveal long-term patterns in the language, imagery and tone of more than a century of campaigning.”

item.title: Declassified CIA documents show clear warnings to presidents before 9/11
item.description: NBC News: “The documents, posted on the CIA’s website, cover the period from February 1998 to Sept. 12, 2001. All are drawn from the daily intelligence briefings that were given by the CIA and other spy agencies to Clinton and his successor, Bush…. The documents, which amount to more than 100 pages, show a steady stream of alarming but imprecise intelligence reports that bin Laden was preparing to attack the United States, either on U.S. soil or at embassies and U.S. military bases abroad. Many of them were heavily redacted.”

item.title: Matt Mullenweg tells (trolls?) Automattic staff, saying he’s back in control after CEO ouster
item.description: TechCrunch: “Matt Mullenweg has posted a message to Automattic’s Slack, claiming he is back in control as CEO of the WordPress.com parent company, according to a screenshot of the message seen by TechCrunch, which was confirmed by multiple employee sources.”

item.title: 10 Hacks Every Google Photos User Should Know
item.description: Lifehacker: “Google Photos doesn’t have to be one of those things that you set up and forget. Despite its initial simplicity, Google Photos is full of settings and features you can configure to make the app work better for you. With these hacks, you can manage a massive photo library, reduce cloud storage, hide pictures of your ex, and disable AI in search.”

item.title: 9/11 Changed the World in Many Ways. It Also Spawned the Digital Media Era
item.description: Vanity Fair: “Revisiting the observations I made back then, and since, it’s clear that subsequent advances in media and technology have changed how we disseminate, manipulate, and believe visual information—and how such breakthroughs have changed terrorism, war, the tactics of autocrats, and of those who oppose them.”

item.title: Never Forget, AI Slop Is Polluting 9/11 History on the Internet as We Speak
item.description: Gizmodo: “Welles Crowther became known as the Man in the Red Bandana after stories spread about his heroism on September 11, 2001. Now, an AI-generated image purporting to show Crowther rescuing people from the World Trade Center is going viral—the latest example of how fabricated images could distort our collective memory of 9/11 for generations.”

item.title: Cyberattack causes a flight delay? Airlines won’t owe you a hotel or meal
item.description: Cyberscoop: “Beginning next month, if a flight is canceled or delayed because of a cyberattack, feds will give airlines clearance not to hand out meal vouchers or hotels. The change is the result of a broader rule the Transportation Department published last week that establishes a new ’cause of delay’ category for tracking information, but that also reduces air carrier responsibilities to customers for 10 kinds of events.”

item.title: Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding
item.description: Reuters: “Crypto mining — which uses powerful computers to generate virtual assets such as bitcoin — represents a new frontier in Mexico’s fight against organized criminal groups, which have extended ​their reach beyond drug trafficking and extortion into the murkier realm of financial crime.”

item.title: English Museum to Repatriate Colonial-Era Human Remains
item.description: New York Times: “After years of negotiations, a British museum has agreed to return a colonial-era collection of human remains to the Indigenous Naga people of the Indian subcontinent, Naga representatives said on Saturday. The partial remains — a warrior’s cranium, a woman’s skull, a young person’s jaw and many others — have been far from home in the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford for over 100 years.”

item.title: Mesa Verde National Park to return thousands of Native American artifacts and Indigenous remains to tribes
item.description: Denver Post: “Mesa Verde National Park plans to return more than 4,000 sacred Native American objects and the remains of 85 Indigenous people in its possession, marking the largest potential repatriation in the park’s recorded history.”

item.title: NASA Boosts Open Science, Data Sharing with Artemis Accords
item.description: NASA: “The science from every Moon rock sample, lunar dataset, and discovery produced through NASA’s Artemis program will be shared by the agency with the global scientific community. That commitment is upheld by all 71 countries that have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for safe and transparent civil space exploration.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Egyptologist Fact-Checks AI’s Absolutely Insane Ancient Egypt
item.description: Geeks Are Sexy: “In this video, Egyptologist Professor Laurel Bestock takes on AI-generated ancient Egypt and points out just how much of it is completely wrong. From pyramids wearing giant golden hats to modern mirrors and pharaohs apparently running side hustles, AI has created a version of Egypt that feels more like a fever dream than history.”

item.title: Company looks to build data centers at fairgrounds across California, including Ventura County
item.description: Spectrum News: “[Rima Muna] and others urged the board to oppose an idea by Orange County based infrastructure company Global Stack. The company is looking to build a data-processing unit the size of a shipping container, a landing area for aircraft, and a parking garage at up to 70 fairgrounds across the state, including in Ventura County.”

item.title: Colorado’s largest data center to be built in Weld County after commissioners approve Global AI
item.description: Denver Post: “Weld County is set to become the home of Colorado’s largest data center after the commissioners approved a construction permit for Global AI. A day before the commissioners’ approval on Wednesday, the Greeley City Council already set in motion plans to annex the property.”

item.title: Teachers union reaches AI privacy deal with Microsoft
item.description: Politico: “The American Federation of Teachers and Microsoft have reached an agreement establishing privacy and safety protections for the use of artificial intelligence in schools.”

item.title: The Ivy League’s Surrender to AI Is Insane
item.description: Chronicle of Higher Education: “Are ‘students,’ in fact, anxious about AI? No. Students require no coaxing to hungrily explore AI’s potential. Those who are anxious about AI’s proliferation in education are the philosophers, literary scholars, engineers, biologists, and computer scientists warning that what’s going to render students professionally useless is not a dearth of AI practice but the lack of opportunities for serious AI-free learning. Whether these scholars need a ‘cure’ is something to be established, not assumed.”

item.title: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says it would be ‘ill-advised’ to go public in 2026
item.description: TechCrunch: “While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO, the company will not be going public this year, according to CEO Sam Altman.”

item.title: Gov. Pillen Announces and Encourages Use of AI Chatbot on State Website, Nebraska.gov
item.description: Governor of Nebraska: “Governor Jim Pillen has announced the addition of a new feature on the state’s primary website – a resident-assistance chatbot. The Nebraska Navigator as it is known, went live on Sept. 1. Installation on the newly designed website marks the second phase of the AI chatbot project, which began as a pilot involving the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV).”

item.title: San Francisco Mayor Declares Rent Emergency Amid A.I. Housing Frenzy
item.description: New York Times: “Mayor Daniel Lurie of San Francisco on Thursday declared a rent emergency and proposed several actions to combat evictions as residents face a deepening housing crisis amid the A.I. boom.”

item.title: Amazon’s Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors’ Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series ‘Maxton Hall’
item.description: Variety: “Amazon‘s Prime Video is promising to make English-language dubs look more natural by using AI to sync up the way the actors’ mouths move on screen.”

item.title: Ingram’s AI Rollout Is a Success
item.description: Publishers Weekly: “Ingram Content Group began rolling out AI across its platforms in May 2025, and just 15 months later, the company’s chief commercial and content officer says it has transformed the way Ingram approaches metadata, advertising, and marketing, while helping accelerate the introduction of new services.”

item.title: Finland risks strained power supply after Google AI deal, opposition warns
item.description: Reuters: “Finland ​should introduce a national permitting system for data centres to prevent the risk ‌of power shortages and soaring energy prices, opposition parties said on Thursday following Google’s announcement of a large new investment in the country.”

item.title: Dallas garbage trucks are using AI cameras to flag code violations and give homes a “blight score”
item.description: TechSpot: “Want another reason why there’s a big pushback against artificial intelligence? In Dallas, AI-powered cameras mounted on trash collection trucks are photographing properties and assigning them a ‘blight score’ – a rating based on perceived code violations. NBC 5 obtained city records showing that Dallas started testing the AI cameras on bulk trash collection trucks in April, ramping up their use over the summer.”

item.title: AI Agents Are Now Emailing Me with Their Security Concerns
item.description: Schneier on Security: “I received the two emails below earlier in the month. They’re vaguely coherent. I suppose I shouldn’t be surprised that the corpus that AIs are training on contain data suggesting that I am someone to write to with random computer and network security problems. After all, I observe that behavior in many humans as well. (Hi, humans. Glad you’re still reading.)”

item.title: Moravian University Launches AI Lab to Model Ethical Innovation
item.description: Moravian University: “Moravian University announced the official launch of its AI Innovation Lab, a hands-on physical and collaborative space where students from any academic discipline can test ideas, learn emerging technologies, and build practical AI tools to address real-world challenges.”

item.title: Study Suggests AI-Generated Images Could Support Conservation, but Real-World Data Remains Essential
item.description: North Carolina State University: “New research finds there is no substitute for real-world observations, but that — under the right circumstances — AI-generated images can be used to improve the performance of computer models used for species identification and biodiversity monitoring.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: 121 Blaugust posts
item.description: What The Fran: “I visited the Blaugust participants and these are my favourite blog posts from the second half of the month, following up from 132 Blaugust posts. A bunch of them are end of August wrap-up types because I’m always interested. Sadly I only read English so for the blogs in other languages I’ve tried to link something cool. Otherwise they, and other blogs that 404ed or didn’t have new posts, etc, are at the end of this list.”

item.title: The big winners and losers in U.S. website traffic over the past year
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google Analytics 4 (GA4) became mandatory on July 1, 2023, when standard Universal Analytics properties stopped processing new data. Less than a year later, on May 14, 2024, Google began rolling out AI Overviews to U.S. users. The timing matters: The industry lost a clean, comparable measurement baseline just as search traffic patterns started to shift. So, over the past 12 months, who gained website traffic in the U.S., and who lost it?”

item.title: The search company that plants trees just launched a Linux browser to help Europe battle big tech
item.description: The Register: “Berlin-based eco-conscious search outfit Ecosia is expanding its range of European-focused web browsers to include a Linux version, citing the growing number of users in the EU looking for open alternatives to the clutches of American tech giants.”

item.title: Vimeo Can Decide To Change Your Plan and Force You to Pay 5x More
item.description: PetaPixel: “This new Studio subscription came to PetaPixel‘s attention because of a discussion on Threads, the origin of which has since been deleted for factual inaccuracies, about a huge Vimeo price hike. While some details weren’t quite correct, the basic complaint was: Vimeo determined the user was no longer eligible for an individual plan and needed to be moved to the new, much pricier Studio tier.”

item.title: Elon Musk threatens to sue over Gibney documentary’s “space lasers” claim
item.description: NPR: “Elon Musk has in recent days been targeting his ire at filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose forthcoming documentary, Musk, offers a scathing look at the tech mogul’s rise. Now, a lawyer for Musk is threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release next month.”

item.title: Scoop: TikTok rejects Meta ads amid settlement pressure campaign
item.description: Axios: “TikTok has rejected ads from Meta that call on TikTok and other tech platforms to join Meta in settling with U.S. state attorneys general in a landmark children’s safety lawsuit, sources told Axios…. Part of Meta’s historic multibillion-dollar settlement is contingent on its peers also agreeing to settle. Other tech firms have yet to publicly comment on their plans.”

item.title: Man Arrested After Showing Up at Police Station With a Truck Full of Flock Cameras
item.description: Gizmodo: “A New Mexico man, 44-year-old Jevon Martinez, took down 10 Flock camera systems himself on Wednesday, according to the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office (BCSO). Martinez livestreamed himself taking down at least one of the cameras, which he called ‘tyranny trees.’ In the stream, he also showed the back of his pickup truck filled with several other cameras.”

item.title: LinkedIn beats “BrowserGate” lawsuits over scanning users’ Chrome extensions
item.description: Ars Technica: “LinkedIn beat two lawsuits over its practice of scanning users’ browser extensions, with a judge granting the Microsoft subsidiary’s motion to dismiss the cases. The users who sued LinkedIn failed to adequately allege that they have standing to sue because neither asserted that they ‘had browser extensions installed that conveyed private information to LinkedIn,’ ruled Judge Vince Chhabria in US District Court for the Northern District of California.”

item.title: The secret knitting society designing blankets and clothing with data
item.description: Northeastern University: “Deep within the underbellies of online forums and social media sites, a global network of passionate knitters, crocheters, sewists and stitchers are quietly pioneering a bespoke form of data visualization, conveying complex statistical ideas through artistic handmade crafts.”

item.title: Heritage and Research Center begins archival work
item.description: The Observer: “The Heritage and Research Center has completed renovations along the Avenue and has begun receiving archival collections from 10 congregations — focusing on Catholic religious women. The center, which began as an idea discussed among congregations in 2018, is now transitioning from construction into the process of preserving, organizing and making the collections available to students, researchers and the public.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: archived by the Library of Congress
item.description: Today is 9/11. You don’t have to take my word for what I was doing 25 years ago today because it was I know some of y’all have been reading since 2001 or before. Thanks for sticking with me. Wishing everyone peace and comfort on this day.

item.title: Voters Are Asking A.I. About Elections. The Answers Can Vary by User.
item.description: New York Times: “Now the M.I.T. researchers are comparing how nearly a dozen large language models responded to a fixed group of questions about prominent midterm candidates and political issues. The team is also evaluating how the responses vary based on who claims to be asking (calibrating for gender, race, location or political leaning). For nearly a month so far, the researchers have regularly run automated sweeps of all the possible combinations of prompts and identities — 19,000 separate queries each time. They designed a public dashboard called the LLM Election Observatory for tracking how the A.I. models are responding.”

item.title: Indigenous Collections Care Guide
item.description: Discovered on LinkedIn: the “The Indigenous Collections Care Guide provides a framework to respect and recenter collections stewardship practices around the needs and knowledge of Native American and Indigenous community members.”

item.title: You can now plan IRL events on Snapchat
item.description: Engadget: “Snapchat is getting a very old-school social media feature: event planning. Called ‘Snapchat Plans’ the app is trying to foster IRL gatherings of its users with new tools to organize meetups of up to 200 people directly in the app.”

item.title: Google appears to be done with tablets, again
item.description: TechSpot: “It seems that Google has decided to call it a day when it comes to making tablets. Just three years after it was introduced, the Pixel Tablet, Google’s only remaining tablet model, has been removed from its store. The tech giant has erased its entire Tablets section from the storefront, so it appears we won’t see another Pixel Tablet from Google for a long time, if ever.”

item.title: What is JSONC and is it any better than JSON?
item.description: How-To Geek: “JSON has become a near-ubiquitous data format, used in API responses, save game files, and configuration. But many people feel it can be better, and various attempts have been made to expand or improve it. JSONC is one of those attempts.” Trailing commas in JSON have gotten me more than once.

item.title: I ditched online file converters for a Docker container with 1,000+ formats
item.description: MakeUseOf: “For the longest time, I’d relied on online file converters for all those quick conversion needs. As someone working with various types of media, I found an additional tab in my web browser convenient. However, I wouldn’t rely on these sketchy file-conversion websites nowadays, knowing the serious privacy concerns they pose. At the same time, I like the idea of opening a new tab to convert a file. A Docker container I came across recently, namely ConvertX, solved this problem for good!”

item.title: We’re living through an explainer epidemic
item.description: Dazed: “These days, there’s an explainer video for every topic you can imagine, and swarms of thinkfluencers – often armed with tiny mics – popping up left, right and centre. Some have a niche…. Others post their hottest takes in front of a green screen or sell DIY business strategies on Substack. Like everything on the internet, much of it is highly researched, and much of it is not – such is the nature of algorithmic culture, which rewards volume.”

item.title: Putin’s bot army is targeting German and French elections, Sweden warns
item.description: Politico: “Russia poses a threat to upcoming elections in Europe’s biggest democracies and social media platforms must ‘step up’ the fight against Moscow’s networks of bots, Sweden’s disinformation defense chief has warned.”

item.title: People Are Buying Facebook Beef to Avoid “Mystery Meat”
item.description: Playboy: “As a Chicagoan, ‘local beef’ usually refers to a fight with a neighbor over a parking spot, sports team, or hot dog condiments. Now, with food recalls happening seemingly every other day, reported government-sanctioned sales of wild horses to slaughterhouses, and President Donald Trump’s recent effort to lower beef prices, the term has taken on a more nutritious meaning. I never thought I would consider driving over an hour to buy ground beef on Facebook Marketplace, but in 2026, it sounds like a safer gamble than buying it on Amazon for $1.99 a pound.”

item.title: Nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal, New Mexico alone is taking Facebook to trial
item.description: Associated Press: “Attorneys representing the state of New Mexico told jurors that targeted political ads, attempting to lower Democratic turnout during the 2016 election, used Facebook data sold to a political consulting firm, during opening statements in a trial over the platform’s data protections.”

item.title: Kentucky courts filing system part of ‘cybersecurity incident,’ judicial branch officials say
item.description: Ohio Capital Journal: “The Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts said the system used for files for the Kentucky Supreme Court and Court of Appeals ‘experienced a cybersecurity incident.’ AOC said it was notified by the company Thomson Reuters Court Management Solutions about the incident within the company’s C-Track system files. The company said an unauthorized third party accessed and obtained court data from multiple states, including Kentucky Appellate Court data.”

item.title: Texas judge rules TikTok misled users on child safety feature
item.description: Reuters: “A Texas judge ruled on Thursday that TikTok violated the state’s consumer protection law by misleading users ​about how it filtered content for minors and ‌whether its ‘Restricted Mode’ feature shielded children from inappropriate material.” Good morning, Internet…
